title: Illustrate and understand the basic layout of financial statements

lessons.title: The income statement
lessons.html:
Why financial statements?

Financial statements are short reports that show how a farm business is doing with money. The farmer, the bank, partners and SARS all use them. There are two main statements you should understand: the income statement and the balance sheet.

The income statement

The income statement shows income and expenses for a period of time, usually one year. It answers the question: Did the farm make a profit or a loss this year?

  • Income is money earned from selling products and services: weaners, milk, eggs, vegetables, contract ploughing.
  • Expenses are the costs of running the farm: feed, seed, fertiliser, medicine, fuel, wages, repairs, electricity, interest.
  • Profit = income minus expenses. If expenses are bigger than income, the result is a loss.

Example: small layer farm, one year

ItemRand
Income
Egg sales420,000
Sale of old hens18,000
Total income438,000
Expenses
Feed250,000
Point-of-lay pullets45,000
Wages60,000
Electricity and water15,000
Egg trays and transport20,000
Total expenses390,000
Net profit48,000

Layout tips: income comes first, then expenses, then profit or loss at the bottom. Group similar items. Show the period covered in the heading, for example Income statement for the year ended 28 February 2026.

The income statement helps the farmer see which costs are biggest. Here feed is more than half of all expenses, so feed price and wastage need close attention.

Keep the income statement for each year. When you compare this year with last year, you can see if income is growing, if any cost has jumped and whether the farm is doing better or worse.

lessons.title: The balance sheet
lessons.html:
The balance sheet

The balance sheet shows what the business owns and what it owes on one specific day, for example 28 February 2026. It is like a photograph of the business on that day.

  • Assets – things the business owns that have value: land, buildings, tractor, bakkie, livestock, feed in store, money in the bank, money customers still owe the farm.
  • Liabilities – what the business owes others: bank loans, overdraft, unpaid accounts at the co-op.
  • Owner's equity (or net worth) – the part that really belongs to the owner: assets minus liabilities.

The balance sheet always balances: Assets = Liabilities + Owner's equity.

Example: the layer farm on 28 February 2026

AssetsRandLiabilities and equityRand
Hen house and equipment300,000Bank loan150,000
Bakkie120,000Co-op account owing30,000
Hens60,000Total liabilities180,000
Feed in store15,000Owner's equity355,000
Cash in bank40,000
Total assets535,000Total535,000

Current and fixed items

  • Current assets are cash or will become cash within a year: cash, feed, stock for sale.
  • Fixed assets last many years: land, buildings, vehicles.
  • Current liabilities must be paid within a year: overdraft, co-op account.
  • Long-term liabilities are paid over many years: a bond or long loan.

How the two statements link

When the farm makes a profit and the owner leaves it in the business, owner's equity grows. Losses make it shrink. Comparing balance sheets from year to year shows whether the business is growing.

Key points

  • The income statement shows income, expenses and profit or loss for a period.
  • The balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and owner's equity on one day.
  • Assets = Liabilities + Owner's equity.
  • Current items turn into cash or must be paid within a year; fixed items last longer.
  • Profits kept in the business increase owner's equity.
